body.text: Two lines are perpendicular if they meet at a right angle (90°), and parallel if they never meet, however far extended, because they point in exactly the same direction and stay the same distance apart. A pair of compasses and a ruler (with no measurements marked, just a straightedge) are the classic tools for constructing these accurately, rather than just sketching by eye.

To construct a 60° angle: draw a line and mark a point on it. Without changing the compass width, draw an arc centred on that point crossing the line, then, using the same width, draw a second arc centred where the first arc crosses the line. The line from the original point to where the two arcs intersect makes a 60° angle with the first line — this works because it builds an equilateral triangle, whose angles are always 60°. A 45° angle is then found by bisecting a constructed 90° angle.

A locus (plural: loci) is the set of all points that satisfy a given rule — the path traced out by a point as it moves under some condition. For example, the locus of points equidistant from a single fixed point is a circle centred on that point; the locus of points equidistant from two fixed points is the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them; the locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines is their angle bisector.

These constructions connect directly to loci: a perpendicular bisector is drawn by finding two points equidistant from both ends of a line segment, and an angle bisector by finding points equidistant from both arms of an angle. Recognising a construction as "the locus of points equidistant from..." explains why the compass-and-straightedge method gives an exact answer rather than an estimate.

The same tools construct regular polygons and quadrilaterals precisely: a square from four equal sides at right angles, a rhombus from four equal sides with two pairs of parallel sides, and a parallelogram from two pairs of parallel, equal-length sides. Always measure and check lengths with a ruler and angles with a protractor once a construction is complete, to confirm the figure matches its definition.
